extracted.intended_audience: potters, ceramicists, ceramic manufactory managers, and students of ceramic production/decoration
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and technical guidance on producing hard (kaolinic) porcelain: raw material preparation, shaping (turning, molding, casting), firing (biscuit and sharp-fire), glazing/enameling, and decorative techniques (sharp-fire colors, enameling-furnace colors, applied pastes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportioning of paste (kaolin vs feldspar) determines properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature of porcelain, its physical and chemical properties, vary infinitely according to the proportion of its two constituent elements (kaolin and feldspar), and as other substances (lime, silicious sands, potsherds, etc.) are added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally, porcelain is more solid as the proportion of clay increases and requires a higher temperature in baking; if the proportion of feldspar is increased it becomes more fusible, may be baked at a lower temperature, and submits more readily to decoration, but plasticity and ease of working diminish rapidly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purification of natural kaolin
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural kaolin is never a pure clay and must be purified before use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purify by pounding the mass and separating components by successive levigations with water — draw off the slow-settling clay first to obtain it almost pure; bray remaining deposits in mills to prepare pastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect mixing / homogeneity of the mixture
rubrics_metrics.description: The mixture of the materials should be perfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When perfectly mixed the mass will keep for a long time and become more plastic as it grows older. Qualities of a good paste may be communicated by diluting and stirring with water and decanting, or by prolonged beating and manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of air-bubbles and achieving plasticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Beating or treading the paste gives it complete plasticity and homogeneity and clears it of air-bubbles which would otherwise swell out in baking and cause much damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attention to this prevents defects that manifest during firing; do not neglect beating/treading as it also conditions working properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shaping on the wheel: staged drying and careful working
rubrics_metrics.description: Clay is first shaped on the wheel into a rough block, left to dry slowly and with care to prevent cracking, then put on the wheel again and carefully worked into the exact shape desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drying must be slow and controlled; final turning performed with simple instruments, keeping in mind that porcelain softens in baking and must be supported later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Molding for complex forms: multi-part molds and seam finishing
rubrics_metrics.description: For reliefs, statuettes, groups, or sumptuous vases the pattern must be divided into parts and as many plaster molds made as parts of the model; the reproductions are joined and cemented with diluted paste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After joining, rub away seams and have the whole finished by a restorer/artist. Consider shrinkage when planning separable parts and mold geometry to allow demolding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for shrinkage in baking (≈10–15%)
rubrics_metrics.description: Porcelain has the property of shrinking when baked; the shrinkage amounts to about ten or fifteen per cent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design, mold division, and fitting must anticipate this shrinkage so parts join correctly and final dimensions are achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting (barbotine) technique and shell formation in plaster molds
rubrics_metrics.description: Pour barbotine into a plaster mold; the mold absorbs water and forms a shell of porcelain-clay adhering to the plaster; when sufficiently thick, pour out the rest of the barbotine and leave shell to dry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small objects are simple; large pieces are delicate — shell must be thicker for larger vessels. The slightest awkwardness may destroy the piece; use measures to prevent separation from plaster (e.g., compressed air or exhausting the outside of the mold).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of compressed air or vacuum to support casting shells in large pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid accidents where the porcelain shell separates from the plaster and falls, introduce compressed air against the interior of the mold when the barbotine is poured out, or exhaust the air on the outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: M. Milet and Delacour's compressed-air method and M. Regnault's exhaust method are cited; these improve adherence of shell and enable clean outlines and surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of absence of seams, purity of outlines, and surface clearness in casting
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence of seams, the purity of the outlines, and the clearness of the surfaces obtained by casting lift the object far above molding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details of casting are exacting; none should be neglected because hidden faults (bubbles, lack of homogeneity) often only appear after baking and decoration and can ruin valuable pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage firing: biscuit-bake then sharp-fire (temperatures and effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Baking is done twice: first at a relatively moderate temperature (1,800° to 2,160°) producing biscuit-baked porcelain; then a second baking in the sharp-fire where feldspar fuses (2,880° to 3,240°).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biscuit-baked porcelain becomes tough and sonorous and is ready for enameling; sharp-fire reaches the fusion of glazing. Trial-pieces should be used to determine the exact moment to stop firing to avoid brittleness or altering porcelain character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enclosing ware in refractory casettes and supporting to prevent deformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Porcelain cannot be baked in direct contact with flames, ashes, and smoke; therefore for both biscuit and sharp-fire it must be enclosed in protecting envelopes called gazettes or casettes of refractory clay, with pieces adjusted on suitable supports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate softening when fitting vessels and arrange supports to prevent deformation while avoiding supports sticking to the piece. Use artifices to support without leaving visible marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slow, regular heating and visual furnace monitoring; use of trial-pieces and slow cooling
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperature should be raised very slowly and very regularly to avoid unequal dilatations which would develop breaks. Heating is watched through openings by observing the color of the fire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Color progression from dark red to white indicates stages; white heat is reached in 24–60 hours depending on furnace. Trial-pieces show glazing and brittleness. After firing, cover the fire, stop vents, and cool by self-cooling over 4–8 days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control furnace atmosphere (reducing vs oxidizing) depending on desired outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: If only white porcelain is baked, an atmosphere of reducing properties is generally best to prevent included iron/titanium from oxidizing and coloring the mass; for decorated porcelain an oxidizing atmosphere is often advantageous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When baking mixed objectives, manage atmosphere by best practices such as introducing gaseous substances adapted to one or the other object; choice of atmosphere affects final coloration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of fuel and movement toward gaseous fuels for better control
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature of fuel is variable (different woods and coals used). Efforts are being made to adopt gaseous fuels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gaseous fuels are preferred for complete mastery over baking due to controllability of atmosphere and heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enamel thickness must be even and adapted to each piece
rubrics_metrics.description: The thickness of the enamel must be adapted to the piece; it may be neither too great nor too little under penalty of accidents; it must be as even as possible, with neither bulges nor thin places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dipping alone cannot obtain required evenness; objects must be retouched with a brush after immersion to correct thickness before sharp-fire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decoration by sharp-fire: qualities, limits, and desirable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Decoration by the sharp-fire consists in application of coloring substances fixed and developed at the same temperature as the porcelain; it gives highly prized results because color is covered by enamel and becomes of one body with the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produces brilliant integrated colors (e.g., Sevres blue) but number of usable colors is limited due to high temperature and some shades are delicate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decoration by enameling-furnace: method and materials (fluxes) and tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Enameling-furnace painting is always done on baked porcelain (enamel) at a relatively low temperature and requires a flux (generally a silicate or silico-borate of lead, or for metals a sub-nitrate of bismuth) to make colors adhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fluxes melt and react with the glaze during firing to fix the color. Some colors require multiple fires. Enameling-furnace colors are rich but typically opaque and cover/hide porcelain's prized qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applied pastes (painting with barbotine) for relief and pictorial effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Applied pastes or painting with barbotine upon raw or biscuit-baked porcelain allows laying a considerable thickness of material which can be chiseled to a fine finish, producing effects like real cameos, and can incorporate coloring oxides to make true pictures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success depends on rightly tempered successive applications. Contribution to decorative value is high, but color range usable in sharp-fire is limited by temperature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent hidden faults in large pieces (air bubbles, inhomogeneity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hidden faults in the interior of a large piece — a bubble of inclosed air, a lack of homogeneity in the paste, or other flaw — are not perceptible till after baking, when the vessel has been decorated, and may become of very great value; the slightest defect in casting may destroy this value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meticulous control of homogeneity and inspection during forming/casting is essential; none of the detailed operations should be neglected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off awareness: material vs decoration (opacity vs translucence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sharp-fire colors are limited and delicate; enameling-furnace colors, though rich, are opaque and cover the porcelain, hiding its prized qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose decoration technique with understanding of how it will interact with the porcelain body and glaze to preserve desired material qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional role: manufactory as research and school (artistic/industrial duty)
rubrics_metrics.description: The manufactory at Sevres, as a national establishment, ought to lay aside the character of a factory and become a school of ceramics, devoting itself to the search for new processes, original forms and decorations, and the creation of master workmen and artists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It should disseminate results to industry and serve as a center for innovation (advisory/policy guidance rather than a production technique).
